title: Physical Science: Chemistry
description: Use particle models and evidence to explain matter, reactions, energy, and chemical systems.

lessons.title: Quantitative evidence and units
lessons.reading: Chemistry connects observable changes to particle-level explanations and mathematical models. Use units, appropriate precision, and controlled comparisons. Density is mass divided by volume; uncertainty limits what a measurement can establish.
lessons.worked: A 24-gram sample occupying 8 mL has density 3 g/mL.

application.prompt: A 10-gram sample has volume 5 mL. Its density is…
application.explanation: Divide mass by volume: 10/5 = 2, retaining the compound unit.

vocab.definition: Mass per unit volume.
A quantified or described limit on the precision or reliability of a result.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: Divide mass by volume: 10/5 = 2, retaining the compound unit.

lessons.title: States, mixtures and separation
lessons.reading: Particles in solids, liquids, and gases differ in arrangement and motion. An element contains one atomic number; a compound has chemically combined elements. Mixtures retain component identities and can be separated using physical-property differences.
lessons.worked: Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid, but not dissolved salt from water.

application.prompt: Which method can recover dissolved salt from saltwater?
options: Use a magnet on all salts
application.explanation: Evaporation removes the solvent, leaving the nonvolatile dissolved solid.

vocab.definition: A substance of chemically combined elements in fixed proportions.
A physical combination of substances with variable composition.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: Evaporation removes the solvent, leaving the nonvolatile dissolved solid.

lessons.title: Atoms, ions and isotopes
lessons.reading: Atomic number is proton count and identifies an element. Isotopes have different neutron counts. Ions differ in electron count from neutral atoms. Average atomic mass is a weighted mean of isotope masses and abundances, not the mass of every atom.

application.prompt: An atom with 11 protons and 10 electrons has charge…
application.explanation: One more proton than electron gives a net charge of +1.

vocab.definition: Atoms of one element with different neutron numbers.
An atom or group with net charge.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: One more proton than electron gives a net charge of +1.

lessons.title: Nuclear change and energy
lessons.reading: Nuclear reactions change nuclei and may change element identity. Conserve mass number and charge when balancing nuclear equations. Radioactive decay has probabilistic individual events but predictable population half-lives. Nuclear processes differ from chemical rearrangements of electrons and bonds.
lessons.worked: After two half-lives, one quarter of an original isotope population remains on average.

application.prompt: A 32-gram isotope sample undergoes three half-lives. How much original isotope remains?
application.explanation: Halve the original-isotope amount three times: 32 → 16 → 8 → 4.

vocab.definition: Spontaneous transformation of an unstable nucleus.
Splitting a heavy nucleus into smaller nuclei.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: Halve the original-isotope amount three times: 32 → 16 → 8 → 4.

lessons.title: Electrons and light
lessons.reading: Electrons occupy quantized energy states. Absorbing suitable energy can excite an electron; transitions to lower states release photons. Photon energy increases with frequency. Emission and absorption spectra reveal characteristic energy differences rather than continuous orbital tracks.
lessons.worked: A higher-frequency photon has more energy because E = hf.

application.prompt: An electron falling to a lower energy state typically…
options: Changes a proton into a neutron
application.explanation: The atom releases the energy difference, often as a photon.

vocab.definition: An electron configuration above the lowest-energy arrangement.
A quantum of electromagnetic radiation.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: The atom releases the energy difference, often as a photon.

lessons.title: Periodic trends and evidence
lessons.reading: Elements in a group have related valence-electron patterns. Across a period, nuclear charge and shielding help explain trends in radius and ionization energy. Trends have exceptions; use relevant data rather than treating them as rules without limits.
lessons.worked: Removing an electron generally requires more energy when it is more strongly attracted to the nucleus.

application.prompt: Elements in the same main-group column often have similar chemistry because of similar…
options: Numbers of occupied shells in all cases
application.explanation: Valence electrons strongly influence bonding and reactions.

vocab.definition: Energy needed to remove an electron from a gaseous species.
An outer-shell electron involved in chemical behavior.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: Valence electrons strongly influence bonding and reactions.

lessons.title: Ionic, covalent and metallic models
lessons.reading: Bonding models explain how particles interact. Ionic substances contain oppositely charged ions; covalent bonds share electron density; metallic bonding involves mobile electrons within a metal structure. Formula units and molecules are not interchangeable descriptions of all substances.
lessons.worked: Molten ionic compounds can conduct because ions move; an ionic crystal's ions are usually fixed in place.

application.prompt: Why can molten sodium chloride conduct electricity?
options: All its bonds disappear into nothing
application.explanation: Mobile charged particles transport charge through the melt.

vocab.definition: A bond involving shared electron density.
Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: Mobile charged particles transport charge through the melt.

lessons.title: Polarity and intermolecular forces
lessons.reading: Molecular polarity depends on bond polarity and geometry. Intermolecular attractions affect boiling points and solubility. Hydrogen bonding is an attraction between molecules or molecular regions, not the covalent O–H bond within water. Structure-property explanations require the correct scale.
lessons.worked: Water is polar, while a symmetrical carbon dioxide molecule has no net dipole.

application.prompt: A stronger intermolecular attraction usually requires more energy to…
application.explanation: Boiling separates particles against intermolecular attractions without generally breaking molecular covalent bonds.

vocab.definition: An attraction between molecules.
An uneven overall distribution of charge within a molecule.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: Boiling separates particles against intermolecular attractions without generally breaking molecular covalent bonds.

lessons.title: Conservation and balanced reactions
lessons.reading: Chemical reactions rearrange atoms. Balance coefficients rather than changing chemical formulas. Atom counts and total charge must be conserved for appropriate equations. Reaction models can describe synthesis, decomposition, combustion, and other patterns without implying that one pattern covers every mechanism.
lessons.worked: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O conserves four H atoms and two O atoms.

application.prompt: Which coefficient of H₂O balances H₂ + O₂ → H₂O with whole-number coefficients?

vocab.definition: A multiplier specifying relative amounts in an equation.
Atoms are rearranged rather than created or destroyed in chemical reactions.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.

lessons.title: Moles and stoichiometry
lessons.reading: A mole connects particle counts with measurable mass. Use molar mass to convert grams to moles and balanced coefficients for mole ratios. A limiting reactant restricts product yield. An empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number atom ratio.
lessons.worked: At about 18 g/mol, 36 grams of water is about 2 moles.

application.prompt: How many moles are in 44 grams of CO₂, with molar mass 44 g/mol?

vocab.definition: An amount containing exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ specified entities.
The reactant that restricts the amount of product formed.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.

lessons.title: Gas relationships
lessons.reading: Gas models relate pressure, volume, temperature, and amount. Use absolute temperature in gas-law ratios. At fixed amount and temperature, pressure and volume vary inversely. Real gases depart from ideal behavior, especially at high pressure or low temperature.
lessons.worked: Doubling a gas volume at constant temperature and amount halves its pressure in the ideal model.

application.prompt: A gas at constant temperature expands from 2 L to 4 L. Its pressure becomes…
application.explanation: For fixed n and T, PV is constant, so doubling V halves P.

vocab.definition: A simplified gas model with negligible particle volume and intermolecular forces.
An absolute-temperature unit.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: For fixed n and T, PV is constant, so doubling V halves P.

lessons.title: Solutions and dissolved particles
lessons.reading: Dissolving depends on particle interactions, temperature, and sometimes pressure. Molarity is moles of solute per liter of solution. Electrolytes form mobile ions in solution. Dissolved particles can shift boiling and freezing behavior; separate concentration from the strength of a solute.
lessons.worked: 0.5 mol of solute in 2 L of solution has molarity 0.25 mol/L.

application.prompt: What is the molarity of 2 moles in 4 liters of solution?
application.explanation: Divide solute moles by total solution volume in liters.

vocab.definition: Moles of solute per liter of solution.
A substance that yields mobile ions when dissolved or melted.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: Divide solute moles by total solution volume in liters.

lessons.title: Energy diagrams and calorimetry
lessons.reading: Breaking bonds requires energy; forming bonds releases energy. The net difference determines whether a reaction absorbs or releases heat overall. For suitable conditions, q = mcΔT relates heat transfer to temperature change. A catalyst lowers activation energy, not the reaction's net energy change.
lessons.worked: An exothermic reaction transfers energy to its surroundings.

application.prompt: Which statement is true about breaking a chemical bond?
application.explanation: Energy is needed to separate bonded particles; bond formation releases energy.

vocab.definition: Releasing energy to the surroundings.
The energy barrier for a reaction pathway.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: Energy is needed to separate bonded particles; bond formation releases energy.

lessons.title: Reaction rates and dynamic equilibrium
lessons.reading: Rate depends on successful particle interactions and factors such as temperature, concentration, surface area, and catalysts. At dynamic equilibrium, forward and reverse rates are equal, not necessarily concentrations. Disturbances can shift equilibrium; a catalyst speeds approach without changing the equilibrium constant.
lessons.worked: A sealed equilibrium mixture continues both forward and reverse reactions.

application.prompt: At chemical equilibrium, which must be equal?
application.explanation: Equal rates keep macroscopic amounts steady even though particle reactions continue.

vocab.definition: A state with equal forward and reverse rates.
A substance changing reaction rate through a lower-energy pathway without net consumption.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: Equal rates keep macroscopic amounts steady even though particle reactions continue.

lessons.title: Acid-base models and pH
lessons.reading: Acid-base models describe proton transfer or related aqueous behavior. Lower pH means greater hydronium concentration. Each pH unit corresponds approximately to a tenfold concentration factor in dilute solutions. Neutralization and titration use reaction ratios, not just equal solution volumes.
lessons.worked: A pH 3 solution has about ten times the hydronium concentration of pH 4.

application.prompt: Compared with pH 5, pH 3 has approximately how much more H₃O⁺?
application.explanation: Two pH units mean 10 × 10, or 100, in the concentration approximation.

vocab.definition: A proton donor in the Brønsted model.
A logarithmic measure related to hydrogen ion activity.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: Two pH units mean 10 × 10, or 100, in the concentration approximation.

lessons.title: Redox and electrochemical cells
lessons.reading: Oxidation loses electrons and reduction gains them. Half-reactions track electron transfer and charge balance. Voltaic cells use spontaneous reactions to produce electrical energy; electrolytic cells use electrical input to drive reactions. Ions and electrons have different paths.

application.prompt: A species gaining electrons is undergoing…
application.explanation: Reduction is electron gain; oxidation is electron loss.

vocab.definition: Loss of electrons.
Gain of electrons.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: Reduction is electron gain; oxidation is electron loss.

lessons.title: Carbon structures and reactions
lessons.reading: Carbon can form chains, rings, and varied functional groups. Structure influences properties, reactivity, and biological function. Isomers share a formula but differ in arrangement. Polymerization links smaller units; a useful material's behavior depends on molecular structure and interactions.
lessons.worked: Ethanol and dimethyl ether share a molecular formula but have different structures and properties.

application.prompt: Compounds with the same molecular formula but different arrangements are…
application.explanation: Isomers differ structurally despite having the same atom counts.

vocab.definition: A compound sharing a formula with another but differing in arrangement.
A structural group associated with characteristic chemical behavior.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: Isomers differ structurally despite having the same atom counts.

lessons.title: Evaluate chemical technologies
lessons.reading: A material or chemical process must satisfy performance criteria within constraints. Evaluate energy use, toxicity, resources, waste, and lifespan rather than one property alone. Scientific evidence supports comparisons, while value judgments may determine which trade-offs are acceptable.
lessons.worked: Compare battery materials by capacity, safety, resource availability, and recyclability.

application.prompt: Which approach best evaluates a new packaging material?
application.explanation: A useful comparison considers multiple stages and outcomes, including trade-offs.

vocab.definition: The stages from resource extraction through use and disposal or reuse.
A measurable desired performance of a solution.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: A useful comparison considers multiple stages and outcomes, including trade-offs.
